articles.title: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.summary: Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife
body: The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.

The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.

The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.

It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.
Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.

Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.

“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.

“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”

Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.

“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.

More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.

Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.

Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.

Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.

Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta, two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.

Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.

Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.

In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on 30 October that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining.
In Oman, divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands.

But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said.

Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.”

Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems.

A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar – the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down – on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea.

Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface.
“Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades – so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy sees ‘window of opportunity’ for peace as US envoys to meet Putin
articles.summary: Ukrainian president says he hopes Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner get ‘specifics’ from Moscow meeting after trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. What we know on day 1,723
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there could be a chance to reach a breakthrough this year in negotiations to end the war, as he arrived in Ireland ahead of talks with US envoys on Thursday. “Today there really is this opportunity, this window of opportunity, when all those participants who are now engaged in the negotiation process genuinely want to achieve a result before 2027,” the Ukrainian president said. He is to meet the US presidential envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, after they return from a meeting with Russian president Vladimir Putin in Moscow. “What’s important is that the Americans flew to Putin with specifics,” Zelenskyy said. “I would very much like them to return to Dublin with specifics.” Putin envoy Kirill ​Dmitriev greeted Witkoff and Kushner when they arrived at a Moscow airport on Thursday morning.

Zelenskyy’s comments came after Russia and Ukraine agreed to the “largest prisoner exchange” of the war at their first US-brokered talks since February – but made little progress towards a broader peace agreement, reports Pjotr Sauer. Both sides sent senior delegations to the two-day talks in Abu Dhabi, led by Kushner and Witkoff. A senior member of Ukraine’s delegation said the Russian team had arrived with “very strict directives” but there had been “big progress” on postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and “I think we have good momentum to bring about a solution before the new year”. Kushner said there was no trust between ⁠the two sides but described the talks as “a good ​first step”.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine hoped for concrete results on resolving the war this year but that much depended ⁠on how ​the US approached Moscow. Speaking alongside Irish prime minister Micheál Martin on Wednesday, he said: “We are living through these massive attacks. Of course we want to get results by ⁠the end of this year, and of course we will be doing everything ​to make that happen. A lot will ‌depend today on the format of the dialogue of the American and Russian ‌sides tomorrow.”

The head of Nato said the Abu Dhabi talks had shown that the US, Ukraine and Europe were “completely aligned and united”, stressing it was now up to Russia to show it would cooperate. “Clearly we have to see that the Russian side is willing to play ball,” Mark Rutte told reporters.

Russia and Ukraine exchanged attacks on each ⁠other’s capitals in the early hours of Thursday. Explosions were reportedly heard ⁠in Kyiv, but it was not immediately clear if ​the city incurred damage. Russia ⁠hit a ⁠munitions ​warehouse ‌in ‌the capital as well as the ‌surrounding region and also struck military ⁠and ⁠energy facilities in Ukraine, the Russian defence ministry said ‌on Telegram. Russia also hit ​a cargo vessel ⁠en route ​to Odesa ​region ports, it ​added. Meanwhile, Russia downed ‌five drones that were heading for Moscow, mayor Sergei ‌Sobyanin said on Telegram. Earlier in the Odesa region, in southern Ukraine, three people died and 11 were injured after Russia launched a daytime attack on a market, local authorities said. Residential buildings were damaged, said Oleh Kiper, head of the regional military administration.

A drone attack ⁠caused a fire in the port area of Ust-Luga by the Baltic ⁠Sea in Russia’s ⁠north-west, injuring ​three workers, regional governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said on Wednesday. Ukraine later said ⁠it had launched the attack on the port, triggering a fire and damaging part ⁠of its network of fuel tanks. “According to preliminary ​information, as a result ‌of drone strikes ‌on the port’s oil infrastructure, the tank network suffered ‌the most damage,” Ukraine’s general staff said, adding that five tanks had sustained damage. A power station had also been cut off, Drozdenko said.

Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation. Kate Lamb reports that the 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to a Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by Ukraine.

A Ukrainian drone strike killed an employee of the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power plant in his home in south-eastern Ukraine, the 15th to be ⁠killed since April, according to the plant’s Russian management on Wednesday.

articles.title: Double amputee marathon runner criticises Badenoch for ‘weaponising his success’
articles.summary: Paralympian Richard Whitehead ‘gobsmacked’ at Tory leader’s speech over proposed £36bn welfare cuts
body: The double amputee marathon runner Richard Whitehead has criticised Kemi Badenoch for “weaponising his sporting success” to justify her proposed £36bn welfare cuts.

The Conservative leader used the example of “double amputees running marathons” in a speech this week to explain the reasoning behind her proposed cuts to disability benefits, which she said were enabling people to “live a life of dependency”.
Whitehead said he had been surprised at her comments and angry that his achievements were being used as part of a campaign to take money “from the most vulnerable that actually need it”.

“I was gobsmacked that somebody’s sporting success would be weaponised in this way,” he said. “To say everybody should work because double-leg amputees run marathons, I was like, wow. It’s very divisive language.

“I understand the welfare system needs a shake-up, but you shouldn’t be blanket taking money away from individuals who need it, it’s their lifeline. There are families out there relying on the support.”
Whitehead has run more than 100 marathons, set world records and won four Paralympic medals over the course of his career, while also completing endurance feats to raise money for charity.
He said several people had sent him clips of Badenoch’s speech on Tuesday and “his mouth was open” as he watched it.

After saying there were “people who genuinely cannot work”, Badenoch went on to say: “The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities, even when they face serious challenges.
“Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world.”

Whitehead immediately expressed his concerns about the comments on social media. “Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day,” he wrote.
“One person’s ability to overcome significant challenges should never be used to justify withdrawing support from others.”
He invited Badenoch to have a conversation with him to learn more about disability and how it had affected his life and how he used his platform to inspire and mentor others.

“She’s utilising somebody’s success and 50 years of hard work for her own means without actually having any knowledge of who I am and the work that I do,” he said. “When I stand on a podium, I use that moment to hopefully inspire and liberate people of all minorities. She’s just looked for a headline.
“I think she needs to really reflect and think about how she communicates with the disabled community, and maybe have a conversation with myself around the work that I’m doing.”

The Conservatives said welfare savings would be made by ending disability living allowance payments to families of children with “milder cases” of behavioural disorders, learning disabilities or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Badenoch said in her speech: “If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself.”

Whitehead said: “I would like a response from her on the terminology she used and I could educate her about the real scenario for people with neurodiversity, with ADHD, who are really struggling. And maybe with that experience she will understand that maybe she’s got it wrong.”

articles.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
articles.summary: Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody
body: A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.

Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.
On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.
Related: Note from Aldo Moro kidnappers sells for €26,000 at controversial auction

The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks from 1969 to 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.
Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.
A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.

“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.
The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.
Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.
Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

articles.title: Millions join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years in protest at housing crisis
articles.summary: Twenty-four-hour stoppage draws high participation weeks before election in which far right could gain power
body: Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
At the centre of Wednesday’s nationwide 24-hour stoppage, singularly called for by tenants’ associations and later backed by workers’ unions, is a pushback against Spain’s deepening housing crisis.

Sandra Mora, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told the broadcaster RNE: “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers – who are also renters or who also pay mortgages – are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill.”

While workers’ unions reported high participation in the strike across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, they said participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions, such as Catalonia and Andalucía, where the soaring cost of housing has been particularly acute.
The Confederation of Tenants’ Association described the strike as a success, saying in a statement that by midday about 4 million people had taken part.

Many schools and universities were reportedly closed or working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, the labour action added to a continuing teachers’ strike that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.

In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks – some with burning tyres – as public transport came to a near-standstill. Pickets were in place soon after the strike began at midnight, blocking off entry to factories, markets and transport hubs. Key roads into Barcelona, including the AP-7 motorway, were blocked off in both directions.

In the evening an immense demonstration filled the city’s main shopping throughfare, with protesters chanting “No more rents! Rent strike now!” and “We’ve brought the country to a standstill, now we’re going to change it.” The organisers claimed 400,000 took part in Barcelona, with local police putting the figure at 55,000. At night small groups of hooded protesters vandalised shops and set fire to rubbish bins, leading to a series of clashes with police.

In Madrid, government officials estimated 120,000 people turned out despite the pouring rain. Scuffles broke out between pickets and police near the country’s main wholesale market, while thousands of demonstrators poured into the city’s main boulevard, halting traffic temporarily. Government officials said more than 50 people had been arrested over minor incidents across the country.

Almudena López, 74, and her husband attended the protest in Madrid thinking of their children. “My son is 43 years old and still doesn’t own a home as he cannot afford one,” López said. She said her son, who works in IT, has to rent a small room in a shared apartment. “When I was young, if you had a university degree, you could get a job by saving a bit – which always required some sacrifice – but you could manage. It’s nothing like it is today.”
Bad weather loomed over plans for afternoon marches after Spain’s state meteorological agency issued 14 alerts for two storms that were expected to bring strong winds, heavy rain and rough seas.

Tens of thousands of people still came together in more than 90 marches, pouring into plazas in Barcelona, Madrid and other cities. The marches in Cádiz, Seville, Córdoba and Huelva had to be cancelled amid forecasts of winds gusting up to 75mph (120km/h). In the evening a downpour quelled the protests in Barcelona and sent nearly everyone home.

The long-simmering frustration at soaring housing prices across Spain burst into public view in September after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the home in which she had lived for more than seven decades.

As protests and encampments sprang up across Spain, it cast a spotlight on a market where properties have been increasingly used as tourist lets, speculative assets and short-term rentals, sending rents rising by 80% within a decade while the cost of homes climbed by 63%.

Before Wednesday’s strike, the tenants’ union of Granada sought to highlight this link, descending on the city’s most touristy areas to vandalise about 300 lockboxes belonging to short-term rentals. “No to capitalists, no to rent-seekers, no to their accomplices,” the organisation wrote on social media, as they posted pictures of lockboxes that had been rendered unusable.

Housing campaigners and unions have called on the government to do more to intervene in the market, with tenants’ unions demanding measures such as a crackdown on housing speculation, the elimination of tourist lets and strengthened protections for renters.

While nominal wages for many across Spain had risen in recent years, Unai Sordo, the head of Spain’s biggest labour union, the Workers’ Commissions, said no amount of collective bargaining would be enough to address housing costs that had climbed by as much as 12% annually. “There is one issue that is fracturing the country, and that is the difficulty many people face in accessing housing,” he told the broadcaster Cadena Ser.

Spain is holding a general election on 29 November. The snap vote was called by the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis.
Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.

While Sánchez has sought to focus the campaign on social issues, the discussion has shifted to questions over infrastructure after at least 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year.

This week Sánchez seized on the strike, whose official slogan is “Salaries. Housing. Prices”, as a way to recast the spotlight, posting a video in which he lauded developments such as the eight-hour work day and national health insurance and credited them to the labour movement and the right to strike. “It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said.
His position sharply contrasted with the discourse of parties on the right who, in the lead-up to the strike, dismissed it as an effort by unions to help Sánchez remain in office.

This week the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, accused striking workers of “holding citizens hostage”. Ayuso, who this year faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office, added: “Everything is chaotic, everything is gridlocked.”

While she acknowledged union activity was a constitutional right, she also took aim at what she described as the “mafia of union representatives” and said she had vented her frustrations to the leader of the People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who polls suggest will be the next prime minister. “I’ll confess something,” she told Spanish television. “I spoke to Feijóo and I told him: ‘Promise me this garbage will end.’”
